title: Loops
intro: Rust has three loops: `for` over a range or collection, `while`, and `loop` (forever, until `break`).

coming_from.go: `for i in 1..4` counts 1, 2, 3 like `for i := 1; i < 4; i++`, `while n > 0` is `for n > 0`, and `loop` is `for {}`. There is no three-part `for` and no `n++`, but `break` can hand back a value from a `loop`.
coming_from.kotlin: Watch the ranges: Rust's `1..4` stops before 4 like Kotlin's `1 until 4`, and Rust's `1..=4` is Kotlin's `1..4`. There is no `n++` (write `n += 1`), and `loop` is `while (true)` where `break` can give back a value.
coming_from.python: `for i in 1..4` is `for i in range(1, 4)` and `loop` is `while True`. The one new thing is that `break tries * 10` can hand a value back out of a `loop`.
coming_from.typescript: Rust has no C-style `for (let i = 1; i < 4; i++)` and no `++`. You loop over a range instead (`for i in 1..4`), and `loop` is `while (true)` where `break` can hand back a value.
coming_from.java: `for i in 1..4` is `for (int i = 1; i < 4; i++)`; Rust has no C-style three-part `for` and no `++`, so you write `n += 1`. `loop` is `while (true)`, except `break` can hand back a value.
coming_from.csharp: `for i in 1..4` is like `foreach (var i in Enumerable.Range(1, 3))`, except that `1..4` gives start and end (4 excluded) where `Range` gives start and count. Rust has no three-part `for` or `++`. `loop` is `while (true)` where `break value` returns a result, so the result can be an ordinary `let` instead of a variable set inside the loop.
coming_from.c: Rust has no three-part `for (init; test; step)`: you loop over a range like `1..4` instead, and `n++` is gone, so write `n += 1`. `loop` is `for (;;)`, and `break` can carry a value out of it.
coming_from.cpp: `for i in 1..4` is a range-based `for` over a half-open range, like `for (int i : std::views::iota(1, 4))` in C++20, and there is no classic three-part `for` or `++`. `loop` is `while (true)` with a `break` that returns a value, so you don't need the lambda trick.

notes: `1..4` is 1, 2, 3: the end is left out. `1..=4` includes the 4.
There is no C-style `for i := 0; i < n; i++`. Use `for i in 0..n`.
`(0..10).rev()` counts down. `(0..10).step_by(2)` skips. A range that starts above its end, like `4..0`, is empty: it does not count down.

faq.q: Can a `for` loop give back a value with `break value`, like `loop` does?
faq.a:
No. Only `loop` can hand back a value with `break value`. A `for` or `while` loop has the value `()`, and the compiler stops you if you write `break value` in one.

The reason: a `for` loop can finish without ever reaching `break`, for example on an empty list. Then there would be no value to assign. A `loop` can only end through `break`, so a value always comes out.

In practice you rarely need either. When you want a value from a loop, use an iterator method. Each one is an expression and says what you mean:

- `find`: the first item that matches. It returns an [Option](/learn/option/), because there might be none.
- `position`: the index of the first match, also an Option.
- `sum`, `count`, `max`, `any`, `all`: one value from the list.
- `map(...).collect()`: a new list.

gotcha.title: Using n++
gotcha.looks_fine: `n++` is normal in most languages you know.
gotcha.why: Rust has no `++` or `--`; `+= 1` is the one way to add one. `++` inside other expressions (like `a[i++] = i`) is a classic source of confusion about what happens first. Go keeps `n++` but only as a statement; Rust drops it.

go.says: Go runs this and prints 1. `n++` is fine in Go as a statement on its own.
go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	n := 0
	n++
	fmt.Println(n)
}

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints 1. In Rust you write the same thing as `n += 1`.

python.says: `n++` is a syntax error in Python, but `++n` runs and prints 0. It is read as two unary pluses, so `n` never changes.
python.code:
n = 0
++n  # n++ is a syntax error; ++n is two unary pluses
print(n)

typescript.says: Prints 1. `n++` is normal TypeScript; Rust has no `++` and wants `n += 1`.

java.says: Java has `++`, so this prints 1. Rust has no `++`; write `n += 1` instead.

csharp.says: `n++` is everyday C# and prints 1. Rust has no `++` and asks for `n += 1`.

c.says: C has `n++`, so this prints 1. In Rust you write `n += 1`.

cpp.says: C++ has `++`, so this prints 1. In Rust you write `n += 1`.

python.code:
# 1, 2, 3 (the end is not included)
for i in range(1, 4):
    print(f"for {i}")

n = 3
while n > 0:
    n -= 1

# no loop-with-value in Python: use while True and set a variable
tries = 0
while True:
    tries += 1
    if tries == 3:
        found = tries * 10
        break
print(f"n={n} found={found}")

check-py.py.code:
assert list(range(4)) == [0, 1, 2, 3]
assert list(range(1, 4)) == [1, 2, 3]
assert list(range(0, 10, 3)) == [0, 3, 6, 9]
assert list(range(3, -1, -1)) == [3, 2, 1, 0]
assert list(range(9, 0, -3)) == [9, 6, 3]
assert list(enumerate(["a", "b"])) == [(0, "a"), (1, "b")]

n = 0
while True:
    n += 1
    if n == 3:
        break
assert n == 3

# the loop variable is a fresh name each pass: changing it lasts one pass (like Rust)
seen = []
for i in range(5):
    if i == 1:
        i += 2
    seen.append(i)
assert seen == [0, 3, 2, 3, 4]
assert list(range(len([5, 6, 7]))) == [0, 1, 2]
print("ok")
